The presented measurements of the beam structure can serve as a basis for the design of microdosimetric measurement setups in clinical ion beams, influencing the choice of acceptable shaping times and detector dimensions. In high-resolution amplitude resolved measurements, achieving sufficient charge resolution in pulse height analysis necessitates prolonged shaping times on the order of 1 µs [37]. To enable single-particle detection at high dose rates and minimize pulse pileup, it is common to reduce the detector cross-section, thereby lowering the average particle rate [38]. However, this method yields only limited suppression of pile-up due to the stochastically distributed particle arrival times. While the average particle rate can be reduced by lowering the cross-sectional area, the probability of pileup remains significant. Even at a low average particle rate, bunching of particles on the ns-scale is observed. These insights should be taken into account for the optimization of readout electronics. ## Characterizing the Delivered Spill Structure of Medical Proton and Carbon-Ion Beams at MedAustron using a High Frequency Silicon Carbide Readout

Matthias Knopf [a,][∗], Andreas Gsponer [b], Matthias Kausel [c,a], Simon Waid [b], Sebastian Onder [b], Stefan Gundacker [b],
Daniel Radmanovac [b], Giulio Magrin [c], Thomas Bergauer [b], Albert Hirtl [a]

_a_ _TU Wien, Atominstitut, Stadionallee 2, 1020 Wien_
_b_ _Institute of High Energy Physics, Austrian Academy of Sciences, Nikolsdorfer Gasse 18, 1050 Vienna, Austria_
_c_ _EBG MedAustron GmbH, Marie-Curie Straße 5, 2700 Wiener Neustadt, Austria_

**Abstract**

Medical synchrotrons are often used for testing instrumentation in high-energy physics or non-clinical research in
medical physics. In many applications of medical synchrotrons, such as microdosimetry and ion imaging, precise
knowledge of the spill structure and instantaneous particle rate is crucial. Conventional ionization chambers, while
omnipresent in clinical settings, suffer from limitations in charge resolution and integration time, making singleparticle detection at high dose rates unfeasible. To address these limitations, we present a beam detection setup based
on a silicon carbide (SiC) sensor and a monolithic microwave integrated circuit (MMIC), capable of detecting single
particles with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) pulse duration of 500 ps. At the MedAustron ion therapy center,
we characterized the spill structure of proton and carbon-ion beams delivered to the irradiation room beyond the
timescale of the maximum ion revolution frequency in the synchrotron. The resulting data offer valuable insights
into the beam intensity at small time scales and demonstrate the capabilities of SiC-based systems for high-flux beam
monitoring.

_Keywords:_ Silicon carbide, beam monitor, high dose rate, medical synchrotron, spill structure, microdosimetry

**1. Introduction**

Radiotherapy using light ions has been recognized as a promising option for the treatment of several types of
cancer, due to the targeted dose delivery and decreased adverse effects on surrounding tissue [1, 2]. Efforts are being
made to further improve the quality of ion beam therapy. This includes, among others, research on higher precision tumor targeting using ion imaging [3] as well as the adoption of microdosimetry [4] into clinical routines for improved
dose control. Further, medical accelerators provide a testing platform for several research areas, including detecto

development for particle physics [5] and radiation studies on space electronics [6]. All these applications rely on
the effects of single particles and thus require precise knowledge of the exact spill characteristics at single-particle
resolution.

Traditionally, in medical accelerator facilities, dosimetry with single-particle precision is not required and challenging to implement at common clinical particle rates up to 10 [10] s [−][1] [7]. Since reliability and durability of the
equipment are the highest priority, beam monitoring is typically performed using gas-filled ionization chambers to
measure the beam intensity [8], while segmented ionization chambers are employed to monitor the beam spot position
and lateral profile [9]. These systems are designed to measure the macroscopic dose delivered during treatment in
accordance with medical specifications, but lack the precision and speed required for certain experiments. The limited
sensitivity of ionization chambers—requiring a minimum charge deposition of several 100 fC [10]—combined with
long charge collection times on the order of 100 µs [11], makes them unsuitable for measurements with high temporal

**2. Materials** & **Methods**

_2.1. The MedAustron facility_

MedAustron is an ion therapy center, located in Wiener Neustadt (Austria), featuring four clinical beamlines as
well as a dedicated research beamline. The facility is centered around a medical synchrotron, based on the proton-ion
medical machine study (PIMMS) [24], with 77.65 m circumference, which allows for the acceleration of protons
from 62.4–800 MeV, [12] C [6][+] ions from 120–402.8 MeV u [−][1] [25] and [4] He [2][+] ions from 39.8–402.8 MeV u [−][1] [26]. The
MedAustron design is optimized to fulfill medical requirements. In clinical operation, the accelerated ions are extracted via betatron core-driven third-order resonant extraction [27]. The particles are extracted in spills lasting
several seconds, which corresponds to a large number of revolutions in the synchrotron. Particle rates obtained in the
irradiation rooms are typically in the range from 10 [9] –10 [10] s [−][1] for protons and 10 [8] –10 [9] s [−][1] for carbon-ions [28, 29].
Due to the influence of power converters on the magnetic fields in the synchrotron, the extracted spill exhibits significant fluctuations in intensity (ripples) in the kHz region [24]. To mitigate these ripples and ensure a constant
particle flux for treatment, MedAustron employs empty bucket channeling [30, 27]. While this technique achieves
a reduction of the intensity ripples, it modulates the spill structure at the timescale of the ion revolution frequency in

∼
the synchrotron ( 1–3 MHz). In clinical treatment, this modulation can be neglected [31]. However, it proves to be
relevant for applications relying on single-particle precision.

_2.2. SiC-based HF readout_

The sensor employed in the detector system was a 4H-SiC p-i-n diode designed by the authors and manufactured
by IMB-CNM-CSIC [32]. In order to achieve readout at high bandwidth (> 1 GHz), the detector capacitance had
to be kept at a minimum. Thus, a small-area circular sensor-design with 140 µm diameter and 50 µm thickness was

2

chosen for the experiment. At full depletion (> 150 V), the measured capacitance was 70 fF. The sensor consists of
an n-doped active region epitaxially grown on a 350 µm substrate [16]. The small surface area of 0.015 mm [2] reduces
the average particle rate of the ion beams sufficiently to allow for a single-particle detection at medical intensities.
